subtopics.title: Economy, Logistics and Infrastructure
subtopics.summary: This group covers the April 2026 Index of Industrial Production (IIP) and the revised IIP series with 2022-23 as the new base year. It also covers the Logistics Port Performance Index for FY 2024-25 and the Zojila Tunnel on the Srinagar-Leh highway. IIP tracks short-term changes in industrial output, while the port index measures operational efficiency across cargo categories.
facts: IIP growth was 4.9% in April 2026, lower than 5.8% in April 2025.
Manufacturing, about 76% of IIP weight, expanded by 6.2% in April 2026.
Mining and quarrying contracted by more than 5% in April 2026.
The revised IIP series uses 2022-23 as base year, replacing 2011-12.
The revised series covers 1,042 products (earlier 839) and 463 item groups (earlier 407).
The revised series adds gas supply, water supply, sewerage and waste management activities.
Logistics Port Performance Index FY 2024-25: Paradip Port tops dry bulk, Sikka Port tops liquid bulk.
Port KPIs include vessel turnaround time, berth idle time, container dwell time and ship berth day output.
World Bank LPI: India's rank in the international shipments category improved from 44 to 22.
Zojila Tunnel is 13.15 km long, expected to be operational in 2028, and is part of a 33 km corridor.

subtopics.title: Environment, Energy and Space
subtopics.summary: The Western Ghats are set to get Ecologically Sensitive Area (ESA) notification, based largely on the Kasturirangan Committee's 2013 recommendations. The group also covers GRAPES-3, an India-Japan study of Earth's upper atmosphere, and the Energy Transition Index 2026 that ranks 120 countries.
facts: The government is set to notify ESAs in the Western Ghats, nearly 13 years after the first draft notification.
The notification is based largely on the K. Kasturirangan Committee (2013) recommendations.
The Kasturirangan approach covers about 56,000 sq km, about 37% of the Western Ghats.
The Western Ghats extend about 1,600 km along the west coast across six states and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
New mining and quarrying projects, thermal power plants and red category industries are restricted in ESAs.
GRAPES-3 is a cosmic-ray observatory at Ooty (Tamil Nadu), operated by the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research.
Researchers from India and Japan used GRAPES-3 to track real-time changes in Earth's upper atmosphere.
The Energy Transition Index 2026 (WEF and Accenture) assesses 120 countries; India moved up two places to 70th.
Six G20 countries are in the Energy Transition Index top 20: Germany 9th, France 10th, UK 11th, China 14th, Brazil 17th, USA 19th.

subtopics.title: Defence and Security
subtopics.summary: This group covers the SIPRI Yearbook 2026 on global militarisation and India's nuclear posture, and the two councils of India's Nuclear Command Authority. It also covers the S-400 and BrahMos systems, other major air and missile defence systems, and a leadership change at the Intelligence Bureau.
facts: SIPRI Yearbook 2026 ranks India as the 5th largest military spender after USA, China, Russia and Germany.
India's defence expenditure rose 8.9% to USD 92.1 billion in 2025.
India's nuclear arsenal reached 190 warheads, including 12 operationally deployed warheads.
The Political Council (chaired by the Prime Minister) is the sole body authorised to release nuclear weapons.
The Executive Council (chaired by the National Security Advisor) gives inputs to the Political Council and executes its directives.
India's nuclear milestones: 1974 Pokhran test, 1998 Operation Shakti, 2003 nuclear doctrine, 2008 NSG waiver.
India received the 4th squadron of S-400 Triumf from Russia; it is called Sudarshan in Indian service.
BrahMos is a supersonic cruise missile (Mach 2.8), jointly developed by DRDO and NPOM, and is conventional only; it was used in combat during Operation Sindoor.
Beaufort Castle, a Crusader-era fortress in southern Lebanon, was under Israeli control from the 1982 invasion until withdrawal in 2000.
Mahesh Dixit was appointed Director of the Intelligence Bureau for a 2-year tenure, succeeding Tapan Kumar Deka.

subtopics.title: Governance, Global Bodies and Peacekeeping
subtopics.summary: This group covers the FCRA Amendment Rules 2026, which tighten compliance for NGOs receiving foreign contributions. It also covers the FATF grey and black lists, the US-led Pax Silica initiative, and India's role in UN Peacekeeping.
facts: The Ministry of Home Affairs notified the FCRA Amendment Rules 2026; the FCRA Act 2010 replaced the 1976 Act.
NGOs must register under one or more of 5 approved categories: social, economic, educational, cultural and religious.
FCRA registration is valid for 5 years and must be renewed before expiry; foreign contributions cannot be transferred to other persons or organisations.
NGOs must utilise at least 75% of previously released foreign funds before receiving the next instalment.
FATF was created in 1989 by the G7 and is headquartered in Paris; Vivek Aggarwal was appointed its next Vice-President, the first time India will hold that post.
FATF grey list covers jurisdictions under increased monitoring; the black list covers high-risk jurisdictions.
Pax Silica is a US-led initiative for secure supply chains of AI-critical technologies; India joined in February 2026.
India is the 4th largest troop contributor to UN Peacekeeping and was the first country to deploy an all-women contingent (2007).
Major Abhilasha Barak received the UN Military Gender Advocate of the Year Award 2025 for work in UNIFIL, Lebanon.
The International Day of UN Peacekeepers is observed on 29 May; the 2026 theme is Invest in Peace.

subtopics.title: Awards, Rankings, Health and Heritage
subtopics.summary: This group covers the Padma Awards 2026 and their rules, the Pradhan Mantri Rashtriya Bal Puraskar and QS World University Rankings 2027. It also covers NFHS-6, International Day of Yoga 2026, the NCERT Dancing Girl restoration, and the proposed UNESCO nomination of Xuanzang's records.
facts: Padma Awards 2026 conferred 131 honours, including 5 Padma Vibhushan, 13 Padma Bhushan and 113 Padma Shri.
Padma Awards were instituted in 1954 and reorganised in 1955 into three categories.
The maximum is 120 awards per year; the cap excludes posthumous awards, foreign nationals, NRIs and OCIs.
Padma selection: recommendation by a committee chaired by the Cabinet Secretary, review by the PM, final approval by the President.
PM Rashtriya Bal Puraskar honoured 19 children (ages 5-18); it was created in 2018 by merging two earlier awards.
QS World University Rankings 2027: MIT retained the top position for the 15th consecutive year; IIT Delhi is India's highest-ranked institution at 118th.
NFHS-6 (2023-24): institutional births rose from 88.6% to 90.6%; stunting declined from 35.5% to 29.3%.
International Day of Yoga 2026 was the 12th edition, held on 21 June with the theme Yoga for Healthy Ageing.
NCERT restored the original image of the Dancing Girl figurine, a bronze statuette of about 4,500 years, excavated from Mohenjo-daro.
India and China are in advanced discussions to jointly nominate Xuanzang's 'Great Tang Records on the Western Regions' for UNESCO recognition.

quizzes.passage: Ecologically Sensitive Areas are zones that the government can notify to protect the natural environment. Once an area is notified, activities that could harm its ecology are regulated, with the aim of conserving biodiversity, forests, wildlife habitats and water resources. Such areas can include forests, biodiversity hotspots, rivers, hills and wetlands. These regions are notified by the environment ministry under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, and the process moves in stages. The Western Ghats, a long range of hills along India's west coast, have been the subject of such a proposal for many years, and the notification is now being prepared. Recommendations made earlier have shaped the proposal. Within these areas, sustainable livelihoods, eco-tourism, traditional agriculture and conservation-based practices are generally allowed. Environmental rules can restrict some heavy-impact activities while leaving room for practices that are less damaging to the land. Space science also draws attention in India. Scientists use ground-based observatories to study particles that arrive from outer space, and collaborations between research teams help them follow changes in the planet's atmosphere. Meanwhile, international reports measure how countries are moving toward energy systems that are secure, sustainable, equitable and affordable. These developments show how environmental protection, scientific research and energy planning appear together in current affairs.

quizzes.passage: The Western Ghats run along India's west coast and are home to rich forests and many species. The government plans to notify Ecologically Sensitive Areas across this range, a step that has been pending for a long time. A draft notification comes before the final one, and such areas can include biodiversity hotspots, wetlands, hills and rivers. Such areas are meant to regulate activities that could damage the environment, so that biodiversity, forests, wildlife habitats, water resources and ecological connectivity are protected. Restrictions apply to some heavy industrial and mining projects, while low-impact practices such as organic farming, rainwater harvesting and eco-tourism remain permitted. In space science, a cosmic-ray observatory in southern India has been used by scientists from more than one country to study the upper atmosphere in near real time. The basic objective of that observatory is to understand the origin, acceleration and propagation of cosmic rays. Such research helps scientists understand how particles from outer space behave. In the field of energy, a global assessment rates countries on how well they are shifting towards systems that are secure, sustainable, equitable and affordable. The assessment covers a large group of nations and offers a yearly snapshot of progress. Together, these topics show the range of environmental, scientific and energy issues in current affairs.

quizzes.passage: The Ministry of Home Affairs has notified new rules for non-governmental organisations that receive contributions from abroad. The rules aim at stricter compliance, transparency and monitoring, and they operate under a law meant to protect India's sovereignty, integrity, security and national interest. Organisations seeking such funds must have their activities placed under defined categories, and they must disclose details about their work, the states where they operate and their public outreach. Certain persons in leadership roles are also covered, as the rules widen the definition of who manages an organisation. Funds are linked to utilisation as well, so an organisation's record of spending earlier money affects whether it receives more. The governing law is also meant to stop foreign money from being used for religious conversion. Separately, an intergovernmental body works against money laundering and the financing of terrorism, and its lists of countries under scrutiny carry different implications for access to financial markets. India also takes part in United Nations peacekeeping, where troops and police are deployed to regions affected by conflict or political instability. Such missions have been recognised with a Nobel Peace Prize, and their personnel are often called Blue Helmets. The broader picture shows how domestic regulation and global cooperation both shape the way resources and peace efforts move across borders.

quizzes.passage: The Ministry of Home Affairs has notified amended rules that tighten compliance for non-governmental organisations receiving money from abroad. Under the governing law, such organisations must register under approved categories, disclose their activities and public materials, and renew their registration before it expires. Registration certificates must specify the purposes and the states or union territories where activities will be carried out. Funds from overseas must first arrive in a designated account at a public sector bank, and they cannot be passed on to other bodies. Other parts of the rules deal with who may hold key roles in an organisation and how spending must be reported. Foreign contributions may be used for religious worship, religious education and community kitchens, but not for religious conversion. Separately, a body based in Europe works on combating money laundering and the financing of terrorism, and it publishes lists of jurisdictions whose systems have weaknesses. The United Nations also runs peacekeeping missions, which involve military, police and civilian personnel. Each year a day is observed in honour of peacekeepers, and the theme for 2026 focuses on investing in peace. Recognition also goes to peacekeepers who work on gender issues in missions, reflecting principles adopted by the UN Security Council to protect women and girls in conflict zones.

quizzes.passage: India's civilian honours recognise achievement across many fields, and the President confers them at a ceremony at Rashtrapati Bhavan. The Padma honours are among the best known of these, and they are given after a multi-stage process. The Padma Vibhushan is India's second highest civilian honour, after the Bharat Ratna. Recommendations come from a committee, the proposals are reviewed at the top level of government, and the final approval rests with the head of state. The Constitution abolishes titles, but the Supreme Court has upheld the Padma honours as recognition of merit and public service rather than as titles, and recipients may not use them as prefixes or suffixes to their names. Government servants are generally not eligible, though doctors and scientists are an exception. The government also honours children each year for achievements in fields such as bravery, innovation and sports, through an award presented at Vigyan Bhawan. University rankings attract similar attention. Such rankings are built on several parameters, including reputation among academics and employers, research output and the share of international students and faculty. The methodology weighs each parameter, so the total score depends on how each parameter is weighted. Both subjects appear in the same part of the current affairs coverage.

quizzes.passage: The Indus Valley Civilisation has left artefacts that continue to draw public attention. One bronze statuette, showing a young woman standing with one hand on her hip, was shown in a school textbook in a changed form before its original image was restored after criticism. It is estimated to be nearly 4,500 years old, and it was made using the lost-wax casting technique. The figurine shows a young female figure standing confidently, wearing a necklace and numerous bangles, and the civilisation it comes from was one of the most prominent urban centres of its era. The statuette is now housed in a national museum in the capital. Heritage also features in cultural cooperation: two countries are preparing a joint proposal to recognise an ancient travel account on a documentary heritage list. That account describes journeys across India and Central Asia during the seventh century CE. In health, a national survey collects data on fertility, nutrition and immunisation, and its latest round reports rising institutional deliveries and lower stunting among children. Yoga is promoted through an annual international observance that coincides with the summer solstice, and the United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution to declare the day. Together, these topics show the variety of heritage, health and cultural issues in current affairs.
